source.title: FearCaut-Qwen: Affective Steering in a Vision-Language Model Shifts the Decision Criterion for Hazard Assessment

record.tranche_reason: The study uses neuron-level selection and interventions as tools for its affect-transfer experiments, but does not test the claim versions about neuron explanation quality, pole-level job shares, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The study reports causal tests of selected affect-sensitive neuron sets, but does not test explanations against held-out activations or score how well explanations predict neuron firing. The cited findings from other work are background, not study results. The neuron-intervention results below concern the claim's subject but fit none of its versions.
record.test_reason: The study picks emotion-sensitive SwiGLU neurons in Qwen2.5-VL-7B and uses knockout, amplification and steering as tools for a hazard-assessment method. It reports no share of neurons with one job, no natural-language explanations or their scoring, no cross-model comparison, no InceptionV1 analysis and no attribution graphs. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that the main result is a criterion shift (Δc −1.515, no gain in d′), which originates mostly during perception (94.4% of the effect).
record.recipe_differences: The study selects sparse neurons and distributed directions for causal emotion and hazard-task interventions. It does not generate or score natural-language neuron explanations, test explanations on held-out activations, or build attribution graphs.

fits_no_version.finding: A sparse set of 256 fear neurons was selectively necessary for source emotion recognition (TSI 27.0). It carried none of the transfer to the building decision, which a distributed residual direction carried instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron sets causally necessary for a source task need not be the units that carry a related downstream effect. The authors put it as "a neuron list is not a circuit".

fits_no_version.finding: Fear neurons overlapped the unsafe-decision and damage-severity neuron sets only at chance level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this VLM, emotion-selective neurons were distinct from the selected structural-decision neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Same-K, layer-matched, magnitude-matched and shuffled-label controls produced near-zero fear-recall effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The source knockout effect was specific to the selected neurons.

record.problems: The paper uses one backbone and one building benchmark; the target test split has 65 cases. The authors also note uneven control depth, including only five draws for the structural random-direction check.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant neuron-intervention result rows left out.

untested.parts: Pole-level shares of one job, two related jobs and not yet understood in Qwen3-32B.
Shares across other dense and mixture-of-experts models and scales.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations drawn from activating examples predict where neurons fire.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity appears only as cited background ("individual neurons are frequently polysemantic"). Selector Jaccard and bootstrap stability concern the selection method, not neuron interpretability.

versions.untested_parts: Pole-level main-job shares and the fraction of poles not understood.
Cross-model or scale comparisons, including dense and mixture-of-experts models.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and interpretability-share estimates across vision models.
Attribution graphs, reconstruction error, and whether they explain model behavior without a trained replacement.
Whether explanations derived from activating examples predict where a neuron fires.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
